html:
In 763 the ruler of the Uyghur Khaganate, Bögü Qaghan, adopted Manichaeism and made it the religion of his state. It is usually called the only state ever to take Manichaeism as its official faith.

Manichaeism was founded in Persia in the 3rd century by the prophet Mani. It taught that the world is a battle between light and darkness, and it spread along the Silk Road, carried largely by Sogdian merchants.

The Uyghurs, Turkic nomads of Mongolia, had been called in by the Tang dynasty to help crush the An Lushan Rebellion. In 762 Bögü Qaghan's army retook the city of Luoyang. There he met Manichaean priests, and he brought four of them home with him. The faith also suited his close Sogdian advisers, who ran much of the khaganate's trade and business.

Bögü was killed in a coup in 779, partly in reaction against the new faith, but Manichaeism soon returned to favour. After the khaganate fell in 840, Uyghurs who moved to the oasis of Turpan kept it alongside Buddhism for several centuries. Manuscripts and paintings from there are among the few Manichaean works that survive anywhere.
